Family Health

Rectocele: bowel emptying, assessment and treatment

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A rectocele is a bulge of the rectum toward the back wall of the vagina. Some cause no trouble; others are associated with pressure or difficulty finishing a bowel movement. Finding a bulge does not prove that it explains every bowel symptom. A useful assessment checks both pelvic support and how the bowel and pelvic-floor muscles work before choosing treatment.

A rectocele is different from rectal prolapse

The rectum is the final part of the large bowel. When the supporting layer between the rectum and vagina weakens, the front wall of the rectum can push toward the posterior, or back, vaginal wall. This may produce a vaginal bulge. Rectal prolapse is a different problem in which rectal tissue moves down and may protrude through the anus.

Other pelvic organs can also lose support. A bladder bulge affects the front vaginal wall; the uterus or the top of the vagina after hysterectomy can descend, and an enterocele involves small bowel. More than one problem can coexist. An examination identifies the affected areas, rather than assuming that every vaginal or anal lump is the same kind of prolapse.

Symptoms do not follow a simple size rule

Possible symptoms include vaginal heaviness or a bulge, discomfort during sex, incomplete emptying and repeated trips to the toilet. Stool may seem trapped despite an urge to pass it. Some people find themselves pressing against the vaginal wall or the area between the vagina and anus to help empty; tell the clinician if you already do this, rather than starting an internal manoeuvre from an online description.

Stool trapping may contribute to later smearing or leakage, but incontinence can have other causes. A small rectocele may be found incidentally, while a larger one does not automatically explain severe constipation. Record what is difficult (hard stool, a blocked feeling, pain, leakage or needing assistance) and how it affects everyday life. Treatment aims at those problems, not simply a measurement.

Why support can change

Pregnancy, vaginal birth and birth injury can contribute, as can ageing, previous pelvic surgery, long-term constipation and repeated straining. Persistent cough and higher body weight may add pressure. These are contributing factors, not a verdict about something you did wrong. Symptoms can occur without a vaginal birth, and having a risk factor does not make surgery inevitable.

Reports also describe rectal outpouchings called rectoceles in men, sometimes alongside prior prostate surgery or problems coordinating the pelvic floor. That is not posterior vaginal prolapse and needs its own colorectal assessment. An older study in selected symptomatic men found an association with prostate surgery; it did not prove that surgery caused every case or establish a general treatment rule.

What the appointment should assess

Explain your bowel pattern, stool consistency, any pressure or bulge, urinary symptoms and pain during sex. Mention childbirth injuries, pelvic operations, medicines and the treatments already tried. A vaginal and sometimes rectal examination can assess support and muscle function. Ask for an explanation and a chaperone if wanted; examination requires your consent, and you can request a pause.

The clinician should consider whether another cause of constipation or leakage is present. These may include medicines, slow movement through the colon or muscles that fail to relax during emptying. Blood in the stool or an unexplained change in bowel habit should not be attributed to a known rectocele without assessment. A gastroenterologist, colorectal surgeon, urogynaecologist or pelvic-health physiotherapist may contribute, depending on the findings.

When bowel-emptying tests are useful

An examination may be sufficient to identify vaginal prolapse; not everyone needs an MRI or X-ray. If troublesome emptying continues despite initial treatment, or the symptoms and examination do not fit together, the team may investigate further. Defecography uses X-rays or MRI to show what happens while you try to empty contrast material placed in the rectum. It can demonstrate trapping, other support changes and movement during evacuation.

Other selected tests assess pressure and coordination around the anus and rectum, or the ability to expel a small balloon. A transit study may investigate how quickly stool moves through the colon. These answer different questions and are not a compulsory package for every bulge. Ask what a proposed test might change in your care; a structural finding on a scan still needs to match the clinical problem.

Make stool easier to pass without forcing it

Bowel care is often the first step. Work toward comfortably soft stools with appropriate fibre, adequate fluids and a plan suited to your health. A clinician or pharmacist can advise whether a laxative is useful; the choice depends on the stool pattern, other medicines and conditions. More fibre or larger drinks are not a guaranteed solution to a muscle-coordination or structural emptying problem.

Respond to the urge to pass stool and avoid long sessions of forceful pushing. If an agreed bowel plan is not helping, ask for review rather than repeatedly escalating remedies. Treat a persistent cough and discuss ways to reduce heavy lifting or activities that provoke pressure. Support with weight management may help when relevant, but these measures cannot promise to reverse a rectocele or prevent every recurrence.

Muscle training and bowel coordination have different jobs

Pelvic-floor training may improve support and symptoms for some people with prolapse. It works best when a trained professional checks contraction and full relaxation, then tailors practice. Repeatedly squeezing harder is not the answer when the muscles tighten instead of releasing for a bowel movement. Report exercises that increase pain, pressure or difficulty emptying.

For confirmed pelvic-floor dyssynergia (poor coordination during defecation) biofeedback can help retrain the timing of muscle activity. This is different from an operation to reinforce the vaginal wall. Treating a coordination problem before considering repair helps clarify how much the rectocele itself contributes. Neither physiotherapy nor a laxative should be presented as a guaranteed way to make the anatomical bulge disappear.

Support pessaries and vaginal estrogen

A professionally fitted support pessary may reduce a vaginal bulge or dragging sensation and can be considered alongside physiotherapy. It supports tissue while in place, rather than permanently repairing it. It may not solve difficult stool emptying, so review that symptom separately. Fitting and ongoing care need an individual plan; report new discomfort or trouble passing urine or stool.

Vaginal estrogen may be offered for menopause-associated dryness or other genitourinary tissue symptoms when appropriate. It is not the same as a support device, and it does not rebuild the supporting wall. Systemic hormone replacement should not be started solely to prevent or cure a rectocele. Discuss medical history and unexplained bleeding before hormone treatment, rather than treating every prolapse symptom with extra estrogen.

When posterior repair is worth discussing

If symptoms remain troublesome after suitable nonsurgical care, discuss whether repair is likely to address your particular problem. A posterior vaginal repair reinforces the tissue layer between vagina and rectum, commonly with stitches using your own tissue. NICE recommends posterior vaginal repair without mesh. Procedures for the top of the vagina, uterus or external rectal prolapse serve different purposes and are not interchangeable rectocele operations.

Ask separately about improvement in the bulge and improvement in bowel emptying: one can improve while the other persists. Risks include bleeding, infection, pain during sex, injury to nearby structures and recurrence. Other approaches may be considered for selected findings by specialists. Future pregnancy plans, health and preferences influence timing. Agree on recovery, bowel care and follow-up instructions rather than assuming a universal lifting or sexual-activity timetable.

Know when to seek help sooner

Get medical advice promptly for a new vaginal or anal bulge, persistent emptying difficulty, leakage or symptoms that worsen despite treatment. With constipation, seek medical care right away for rectal bleeding or blood in stool, constant abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting, fever, lower-back pain or unexplained weight loss. Any one of these is a reason to seek assessment; do not wait for the entire list.

Get emergency help if you suddenly cannot pass urine or if prolapsed rectal tissue is stuck outside the anus. Heavy bleeding also needs immediate help. Do not assume these are routine rectocele symptoms or wait for a physiotherapy appointment. For ongoing care, agree on goals and a review date so that persistent symptoms lead to reassessment rather than an endless cycle of straining and self-treatment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Describe bulge and bowel symptoms separately so treatment targets the difficulties that matter to you.

Ask whether stool consistency, coordination and other pelvic findings have been assessed before considering surgery.

Agree on treatment goals, a review date and clear instructions for warning symptoms.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organise bowel-pattern notes, previous treatments, questions and review dates. BeMama cannot identify the cause of a bulge, interpret defecography or choose an exercise, pessary or operation for you.

When to seek help

Seek care right away for constipation with bleeding, constant abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting, fever, lower-back pain or unexplained weight loss. Sudden inability to urinate or trapped rectal prolapse needs emergency help; heavy bleeding requires immediate help. Do not assume new symptoms are explained by a known rectocele.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Rectocele bulges toward the vagina; external rectal prolapse comes through the anus.
  • The finding and its size do not automatically explain every bowel symptom.
  • Bowel care and treatment of muscle-coordination problems often come before repair.
  • A pessary supports tissue, and vaginal estrogen treats selected tissue symptoms; neither guarantees anatomical cure.
  • Surgery should have clear symptom goals, with realistic discussion of bowel outcomes, risks and recurrence.

Frequently asked questions

Can a mild rectocele cause no symptoms?

Yes. Some are found during an examination for another reason and need no active treatment if they are not troublesome. A percentage found on examination is not the same as the proportion of people who have symptoms or need surgery.

What can a troublesome rectocele feel like?

It may cause a vaginal bulge, pressure, incomplete stool emptying, repeated attempts to pass stool or later smearing. Severity cannot be judged from one symptom or size alone. Tissue coming through the anus needs assessment for a separate problem such as rectal prolapse.

Is rectocele possible in men?

Rectal outpouchings with this name have been reported in men, but they are not posterior vaginal prolapse. Older studies in selected patients describe coexisting muscle-coordination problems and previous prostate surgery. Those findings do not establish a universal cause or treatment. Persistent symptoms need individual colorectal assessment.

What can I do at home?

Follow an agreed plan to keep stool comfortable to pass, avoid prolonged forceful straining and seek treatment for persistent cough or constipation. Adapt activities that provoke pressure. Pelvic-floor exercises should fit your assessed muscle function. Home care may improve symptoms but does not guarantee that the rectocele will disappear.

Does everyone need defecography?

No. Vaginal prolapse can often be identified by examination. Dynamic imaging or pressure and balloon tests are selected when they can help explain persistent emptying problems or guide treatment, rather than ordered solely because a bulge exists.

Will surgery cure constipation?

It may help when the rectocele is contributing to emptying difficulty, but constipation can persist because of muscle coordination, slow transit or another cause. Ask which symptoms the planned repair is expected to improve and what care will continue afterward.

Can hormones or a pessary repair the weakened wall?

A support pessary holds tissue in place while it is used; vaginal estrogen may help selected menopause-associated tissue symptoms. Neither is a guaranteed structural repair. Systemic hormone treatment is not a rectocele-prevention or cure plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
